summary: An IAB statement that, even though RFC 1597 reserves address space for private networks, any enterprise that expects to connect to the Internet should apply for globally unique addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo advises organizations that anticipate Internet connectivity to seek globally unique addresses under the allocation criteria. It distinguishes those addresses from private space intended for networks that remain isolated.

subtitle: IAB guidance on IP address allocation for enterprises that expect Internet connectivity.

tldr.problem: Private address space is intended for isolated networks, while organizations that expect Internet connectivity need addresses that distinguish their destinations globally.
tldr.mechanism: The memo advises registries to apply RFC 1466 allocation criteria and says the existence of private address space should not prevent an eligible enterprise from requesting globally unique addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1814 is Informational guidance. It warns that a globally unique address alone does not guarantee that every provider will route it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1814 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo provides address-allocation guidance referencing RFC 1466 and RFC 1597.

sections.title: Private and Globally Unique Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 1814 was submitted on behalf of the IAB and IANA to guide Internet registries in applying RFC 1466 and RFC 1597. RFC 1597 reserves addresses for private networks that are isolated and will remain isolated from the Internet.

The memo says the existence of private address space should not prevent an enterprise from obtaining public address space when it meets the allocation criteria. Registries may require an engineering plan and attention to address conservation.
sections.plainLanguage: Private address space is for networks intended to stay separate from the Internet. An organization that expects outside connectivity should consider applying for globally unique addresses.

sections.title: Guidance for Different Organizations
sections.content:
An enterprise with many hosts that may need external IP connectivity should apply to an Internet registry for a block of globally unique addresses. A small or medium enterprise can use globally unique addresses assigned by its service provider when available.

If a smaller enterprise wants unique addresses and cannot obtain them from a provider under reasonable conditions, or has no provider, registries are recommended to assign addresses without tying them to provider choice. The RFC says an engineering plan may document a realistic deployment schedule and address conservation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes different paths to address allocation depending on the organization's size and service-provider situation. Applicants may need to explain their deployment plans and expected address needs.

sections.title: Connectivity Is Not Guaranteed
sections.content:
Addresses from RFC 1597 should not be routed by the Internet. The memo says organizations that anticipate external connectivity should apply for globally unique addresses so Internet destinations can be distinguished.

A globally unique address does not guarantee Internet-wide connectivity. Service providers may restrict which addresses they route, and some may require an enterprise to renumber as a condition of connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: A unique address helps identify an Internet destination, but providers decide what routes they carry. An organization may still need to meet a provider's routing conditions.
